content: The data suggests that there is a probable increase in the risk of abnormal AST (aspartate aminotransferase) elevation when using ASPY (artesunate-pyronaridine) compared to other antimalarial treatments. This conclusion is based on data from 6,417 participants across seven randomized controlled trials. The difference observed was 4 more cases per 1,000 individuals treated, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0 fewer to 10 more cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. For bilirubin levels, there is likely little to no difference between ASPY and other antimalarial treatments. This conclusion is based on data from 1,649 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference observed was 4 more cases per 1,000 individuals treated, with a 95% CI ranging from 2 fewer to 5 more cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. There may be an increased risk of elevated ALT (alanine aminotransferase) with subsequent treatments using ASPY compared to other antimalarial drugs. This conclusion is based on data from 1,649 participants in one randomized controlled trial. The difference observed was 5 more cases per 1,000 individuals treated, with a 95% CI ranging from 1 fewer to 21 more cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence is low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. The systematic review included studies such as Poravuth 2011, Shin 2011, Rueangweerayut 2012, Tshefu 2010, Roth 2018a, Nelwan 2015, and Kayentao 2012. The baseline comparator used was the control arm of the reference intervention. There was no serious inconsistency or indirectness noted, but serious imprecision was identified in the data. In another systematic review, studies such as Sagara 2018 (conducted in multiple locations including Mali, Burkina Faso, and Guinea), Poravuth 2011, Shin 2011, and others were included. The baseline comparator was again the control arm of the reference intervention. No serious inconsistency or indirectness was noted, but serious imprecision was identified. The confidence intervals included both negligible effects and clinically significant effects. For uncomplicated malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, four trials conducted in children in The Gambia, Kenya, Malawi, and Uganda showed reductions in parasitemia with three days of artesunate treatment. The trials used consistent screening methods and inclusion criteria, with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine as the partner antimalarial drug. Resistance to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine was noted at three study sites, with parasitological failure rates of 10–13% in The Gambia, 27% in Kenya, and 25% in Uganda. The confidence intervals were narrow and included clinically important effects, indicating no serious imprecision. For reducing the transmissibility of treated P. falciparum infections in low-transmission areas, a single trial with 223 participants showed that a 0.25 mg/kg dose of primaquine may rapidly reduce gametocyte infectivity to mosquitoes. However, the evidence was downgraded due to very serious imprecision and indirectness, as the trial was conducted in a single setting with few events. In terms of hemoglobin (Hb) changes, one study with 101 participants showed a mean drop in Hb of 15% in the control group treated with ACT (artemisinin-based combination therapy) alone, compared to a 3% lower mean drop in the intervention group treated with ACT plus primaquine. The certainty of evidence was low due to very serious indirectness. For uncomplicated hyperparasitemia, data from 12 studies involving 1,439 participants showed that artemether-lumefantrine (AL) may reduce fetal loss and major congenital anomalies compared to quinine. The difference observed was 37 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals treated, with a 95% CI ranging from 56 fewer to 8 fewer cases per 1,000. The certainty of evidence was low, and upgrading the evidence was not appropriate due to overlapping confidence intervals with smaller effects. In summary, while ASPY and other antimalarial treatments show some differences in liver enzyme elevations and hemoglobin changes, the evidence is often limited by imprecision, indirectness, and variability in study settings. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and provide more robust conclusions.
